name: Jamal Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a wheel loader at a large mine, feeding the crushing line from a pile of rock. I'm 43 and fairly new to the work, so I watch the older operator's hand signals when the pile slumps; I'm still learning what a safe face looks like. The best part is a smooth feed with no blockage. My partner Nia works at a community clinic reception desk, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. My mine pay is better than the usual rate and we've saved over six months of expenses, though the clinic income still matters to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little AI in the office won't change the way I feed the crusher. I use an AI tool sometimes when the maintenance sheet has a term I don't understand, then ask the fitter before trying anything with the loader. A screen can explain a word, but it cannot see the pile move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my mine shifts and Nia's clinic reception hours to continue if the change stays small. We have enough savings for more than six months of bills, and the mortgage is manageable on our two incomes. I'd still be careful about overtime promises, because I know my higher rate depends on this job lasting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the loader shifts and checking the pile with the older operator before the first bucket. Tonight Nia and I would review the children's school costs beside the mortgage, just as we do each term. In the first year I'd use the same maintenance sheet and check unfamiliar words with the fitter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm enough about our income to think about ordinary work. I am more bothered by a sudden slump in the rock pile than by a small saving at a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the pile slumps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I stop the loader and call the older operator over. I do not try to make up lost time by reaching into a face I haven't judged properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do school costs show up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children both need bus tickets, and one has a music lesson. We count those before we talk about holidays, not after.

say: I would say **minor office AI** leaves loader work largely as it is.
I check unfamiliar sheet terms with the **fitter** before touching the machine.
think: I expect my shifts and Nia’s **clinic hours** to continue.
Our **six-month savings** and two incomes make the mortgage manageable.
do: Keep taking **loader shifts** and inspect the pile before the first bucket.
Review **school costs** with Nia beside the mortgage this term.
feel: **Calm** about income and focused on physical safety.
S0.quote: A screen can explain a word, but it cannot see the pile move.
fieldNote: Jamal’s cautious AI use supplements a **fitter’s judgement** and an experienced operator’s ground check.
His strong savings and steady household earnings support **calm**, while current school costs remain real.

steps.text: Keep taking loader shifts and inspect the rock pile before each first bucket

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my crew that planning and booking software may reach Nia's reception desk before anyone replaces a loader. At our mine, I would want to see whether a new feed plan keeps the crusher moving safely. If it does, I can learn it after a proper trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nia handles bookings and customer questions at the clinic, so her hours could shrink sooner than mine. My junior position could also mean a missed shift if the mine needs fewer loaders after smarter planning. Savings give us room, but the mortgage was set for two wages, not a guess about how much one wage might stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Nia to check the clinic's proposed rota and training options with her manager. At the mine I'd watch a senior operator use any new feed plan for two weeks before trying it myself. If either set of hours drops in the first year, I'd apply to one of the many nearby mines and we'd hold off on replacing our living room furniture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel concerned about Nia first and then about my own shifts. A tested plan is interesting. An empty square on the clinic rota is personal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Nia ask about training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether she can move into patient-facing work that still has paid hours. She likes helping people find the right room more than entering bookings, but she needs the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the feed plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd put the actual crusher stops beside the plan for two weeks. If the screen says the pile is fine while the loader has to stop, the screen needs fixing.

say: I would say **clinic bookings** may change before loader work does.
I would try a new **feed plan** after a proper safety trial.
think: Nia’s **reception hours** could shrink before my physical shifts do.
My junior grade also leaves room for **lost loader hours**.
do: Ask Nia to check the **clinic rota** and paid training options.
Watch a senior operator test the **feed plan** for two weeks.
Apply to a **nearby mine** and delay furniture if either wage falls.
feel: **Concerned** about Nia’s hours and my own junior roster.
S1.quote: An empty square on the clinic rota is personal.
fieldNote: The clinic’s booking work creates an **early household exposure** that the loader itself does not share.
Jamal is willing to adopt the feed plan only after **two weeks of evidence**.

steps.text: Test the AI feed plan after a senior operator runs it for two weeks
Apply to a nearby mine if either household wage falls
Delay replacing living room furniture if either wage falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 could take much of Nia's booking work, while a loader that works as well as a person comes about three years later, around 2031. We need to plan for two separate shocks to our household. I wouldn't ask the children to understand a robot timetable, but I would expect the clinic and mine to explain it to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nia might lose hours quickly, and I could lose the loader seat in 2031. Even with a good savings account, two lost wages would put the mortgage in danger after a while. I'm junior at mining, so the idea that I can walk into a technical job tomorrow is too easy by half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with Nia this week and list which clinic tasks are bookings and which involve helping patients in person. I'd ask the mine's training officer whether a paid equipment inspection place exists and keep taking loader shifts for now. In 2029 I'd apply for that place if paid, and I'd send applications to nearby mines hiring operators. If robots take the loader in 2031, I'd take paid inspection work if I'd earned it, or keep searching with the savings as a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the chance that both pay packets go, and I lie awake some nights counting mortgage payments. I can make a plan, but the short interval leaves little room for a wrong turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the clinic list help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nia could take the list to her manager and ask where the patient-facing hours are going. The list wouldn't make a job appear, but it would make the conversation specific.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would inspection work survive robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Machines still need checks, but I would ask about actual paid vacancies and not call it a safe trade for life.

say: I would separate **2028 booking AI** from capable mining robots around **2031**.
I would ask the **clinic and mine** for clear plans affecting our wages.
think: Nia could lose hours early, and my **loader seat** could go in 2031.
Two lost wages could exhaust even our **strong savings** against the mortgage.
do: List Nia’s **booking and patient tasks** with her this week.
Ask about a **paid inspection place** and keep loader shifts.
Apply in 2029 for paid training and **nearby operator jobs**.
feel: **Anxious** about two possible lost wages and sleepless mortgage calculations.
S2.quote: The list wouldn't make a job appear, but it would make the conversation specific.
fieldNote: The fast scenario threatens **clinic desk work** before capable robots threaten Jamal’s hands-on loader work.
He has a plan and savings, but expects **two wage losses** and describes sleepless mortgage arithmetic.

steps.text: Keep taking loader shifts while the mine still pays drivers
Apply in 2029 for paid equipment inspection training if offered
Send applications to nearby mines hiring loader operators in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people five years gives both employers time to say what will happen to paid hours. Thinking AI changes Nia's desk work in 2031, then capable loaders could arrive at my mine around 2034. I would want the mine to test the machines with operators present before changing the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 at the first date and 51 when the robots reach loader work. Our children will be older and maybe need different support, while the mortgage may still be running. I could learn inspection slowly over several years if someone pays me to practise, but I cannot assume a certificate buys a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Nia to seek a paid patient support pathway at the clinic while bookings still need people. I'd shadow our mine fitter for a half-day each month and write down what I understand from each inspection. In 2032 I'd check actual paid inspection places and apply if one opens; meanwhile I'd keep my loader shifts. If none opens by 2034, I'd apply to nearby mines with human operators before giving up the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, but I can see a sequence instead of a cliff. Five years would let us find out whether the clinic and mine actually honour their offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you shadow first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fitter's tyre and hydraulic checks, because I know the loader and can see what she is testing. I would not call myself a mechanic after watching one shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change your mind about a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written wage during training and a record of graduates getting paid jobs. I'm open to it when those facts are visible.

say: I would say **2031 AI** and **2034 robots** require separate employer plans.
Operators should witness **machine tests** before rosters change.
think: At 51, I may still need wages for **mortgage and older children**.
A certificate matters only if it leads to **paid inspection work**.
do: Ask Nia to explore **paid patient support** at the clinic.
Shadow the mine fitter monthly while **keeping loader shifts**.
Check paid places in 2032 and apply to **nearby mines** if needed.
feel: **Uneasy**, but able to see a sequence of options.
S3.quote: I would not call myself a mechanic after watching one shift.
fieldNote: Jamal accepts a new trade once a **wages and jobs** make the offer credible.
He plans for both earners and keeps **loader income** through the slower transition.

steps.text: Shadow the mine fitter for half a day each month
Keep taking loader shifts through the inspection trial
Apply to nearby mines if no paid inspection place opens by 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the extra time is useful if we check the plans each year. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, and loaders that can do my physical work as well as people arrive around 2039. A decade is long enough to learn something, though it can also be spent waiting for a noticeboard update.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when Nia's desk work changes and 56 when capable robots can take my loader shifts. The children should be grown and their school costs behind us, but the mortgage might remain and neither of us has promised income at 56. Our savings and other local mines give choices, not an automatic retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and use the mine's proven feed planning tool after an operator has tested it. Nia and I would put a fixed extra amount from my higher wage against the mortgage, leaving the savings buffer intact. In 2037 I'd apply for paid inspection shifts at this mine and compare offers at nearby sites. By 2039 I'd take the best paid work we could verify, rather than count on a pension I haven't checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly steady with a decade to act. I still want an annual check on wages, vacancies and the mortgage, because time can slip past without a decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an annual check look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit down after the mortgage statement arrives and write down the balance, our actual wages, and mine vacancies. I want numbers on one page, not a hopeful conversation in the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children follow you into mining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show them what the work pays and how quickly the equipment is changing. They can choose a trade, but I wouldn't promise my loader will still have a human seat.

say: I would ask for **annual plans** through the 2036 office and 2039 robot changes.
A decade permits learning, but **waiting** can waste it.
think: At 56, grown children may cost less, while **mortgage and wages** remain uncertain.
Savings and local mines provide options, not **automatic retirement**.
do: Keep driving and use a **tested feed tool**.
Pay extra **mortgage principal** from higher wages while preserving savings.
Apply for **paid inspection shifts** in 2037 and compare nearby offers.
S4.quote: I want numbers on one page, not a hopeful conversation in the car.
fieldNote: Jamal balances proven technology with **vacancies and wages** over the decade.
He expects paid work at 56 and treats **school costs** as likely ended by then.

steps.text: Keep driving the loader while paid shifts remain
Use the tested AI feed planning tool after operator review
Pay fixed extra mortgage principal from higher wages

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because Nia's clinic hours could shrink before the mine's loader robots arrive in 2031. Paid clinic training for patient work, a real mine inspection place, and clear dates from both employers would help. Our savings can bridge a gap, but they cannot be the family wage forever.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether both employers would change shifts in the same month. We could manage one lower pay slip while the other stayed steady. Two lower pay slips on the same kitchen table would be a different problem.

headlineQuote: Two lower pay slips on the same kitchen table would be a different problem.
portrait: Jamal is a **43-year-old junior loader operator** who checks unstable rock with experienced colleagues.
His **higher mine wage** and six-month savings support two school-age children and a mortgage.
He uses AI occasionally after **operator testing**, while Nia’s clinic bookings face earlier thinking AI.
He seeks **paid inspection work** and checks both household wages across the three AGI timelines.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** because clinic hours may fall before capable loaders reach the mine around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid clinic training**, a mine inspection place and clear dates from both employers would protect the household.
